0.note: See how you translated the term “chief musician” in the superscription to Psalm 4. Alternate translation: [For the leader of worship music] or [For the music director]

See how you translated the similar expression “On Sheminith” in the superscription to Psalm 6. Alternate translation: [Set to the tune Yonath Elem Rehoqim] or [Perform in the Yonath Elem Rehoqim style]

The words that the ULT translates as **A Faraway Silent Dove** could also mean “A Dove on Distant Oaks.” If a translation of the Bible exists in your region, you may wish to use the reading that it uses. If a translation of the Bible does not exist in your region, you may wish to use the reading of the ULT. Alternate translation: [A Dove on Distant Oaks]

The superscription to this psalm identifies it as a **miktam**. Since the meaning of this word is not certain, you may wish to represent it in its Hebrew form and spell it the way it sounds in your language. See the discussion of that term in the Introduction to Psalms.

This superscription is referring to events related in 1 Samuel 21:10–15. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could describe these events more fully. Alternate translation: [David wrote this song when he fled from Saul to the Philistine city of Gath, hoping he would be safe there, but the Philistines seized him]

1.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [Man tramples me, so be gracious to me, God!]

This is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. Use a form in your language that communicates a polite request, here and in verses 7 and 8. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [Please be gracious to me]

David is not referring to a specific **man**. He means all of the Philistines who have captured him. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [men are trampling me] or [people are trampling me]

David is speaking as if the Philistines were actually trampling on him. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly, here and in the next verse. Alternate translation: [men are harassing me] or [people are harassing me]

David is using the term **day** to mean “time,” since time consists of days. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly, here and in verses 2 and 5. Alternate translation: [All the time] or [Continually]

The words **fighting** and **oppresses** together express a single idea. David is using the word **fighting** to tell in what way **man** (representing his human opponents) **oppresses** him. If it would be more natural in your language, you could express this meaning in a different way. Alternate translation: [he oppresses me hostilely] or [they oppress me hostilely]

2.q: שָׁאֲפ֣וּ שׁ֭וֹרְרַ⁠י כָּל־הַ⁠יּ֑וֹם כִּֽי־רַבִּ֨ים לֹחֲמִ֖ים לִ֣⁠י מָרֽוֹם
2.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [Because many are fighting against me arrogantly, my enemies trample me all of the day]

3.note: David is stating the pronoun **I** separately, even though the verb translated as **I will trust** already includes this meaning. He is doing that to express a commitment or resolve. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [I am resolved that the day I fear, I will trust in you]

David is using **The day** as a common expression of his culture to describe the occasion on which something might happen. If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [If ever] or [When]

4.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put David’s statement **I praise his word** at the beginning of this verse so that it does not interrupt his statement **In God … I trust**. However, it is for emphasis and emotional impact that David introduces the information that he praises God’s word in the middle of the information that he trusts God, so if you move the former information to the beginning of the verse, you should try to convey the emphasis and emotional impact in another way. Alternate translation: [I praise God’s word, so I trust completely in him] or [I celebrate God’s promises, so I trust completely in him]

David is using the term **word** to represent **God** speaking to him by using words. If it would be clearer in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I praise him for what he has said to me] or [I praise him for his promise to me]

Here, **flesh** represents human beings, who are made of flesh. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [What will human beings do to me?]

David is using the question form for emphasis. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [Human beings can certainly do nothing to me!]

5.note: The term that the ULT translates as **matters** can also mean “words.” So this could mean: (1) that the people David is describing are causing trouble in his affairs. Alternate translation: [they cause trouble in my affairs] or (2) that these people are figuratively reshaping, that is, distorting, what David says. Alternate translation: [they twist my words]

David is saying **all** as an overstatement for emphasis. He is referring not to every thought that his Philistine captors have but to **all of their thoughts** about him. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [all of their thoughts about me]

6.note: David is stating the pronoun **they** separately, even though the verb translated as **they watch** already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize the personal role that his enemies are taking in watching him. (They are not appointing others as spies but doing the spying themselves.) If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [they personally watch] or [it is they who watch]

David is using his **heels** to represent how he walks on his feet to go places. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. You could also use plain language. Alternate translation: [they watch my steps] or [they observe where I go]

Here, David’s **life** represents an opportunity to take his life or kill him. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. The UST models one way to do that.

7.note: The word that the ULT translates as **Upon** could indicate: (1) that **iniquity** characterizes David’s enemies. Alternate translation: [Because of their iniquity, shall there be an escape for them] or (2) that **iniquity** is the means that David’s enemies would use to **escape** from the just consequences of their actions. Alternate translation: [Shall there be an escape for them by iniquity]

David is using the question form for emphasis. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [Because of their iniquity, there should not be an escape for them!] or [There should not be an escape for them by iniquity!]
Here the **nose** represents anger. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [In anger]

David is speaking as if the **peoples** were actually in an elevated position and God would **make** them **go down** from there. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [destroy the peoples]

8.note: David is stating the pronoun **you** separately, even though the verb translated as **you record** already includes this meaning. He is doing that in order to emphasize a contrast between what his enemies are doing to try to harm him and what God is doing to watch over him and care for him. Alternate translation: [But for your part, you record]

David is speaking as if God had actually recorded his **wandering**, that is, as if God had written down that at this point David had left Israel to live among the Philistines. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [you are aware of my wandering]

David is speaking as if God actually had a leather **bag** that held fluids, such as people in this culture used to hold water or wine when traveling through arid regions, and that he wanted God to put his **tears** in it. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Keep my tears close to you]

David is using his **tears** to represent the sorrows he has experienced. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [Always be mindful of my sorrows]

David is using the question form to make a confident affirmation. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [After all, they are in your record.]

Earlier in this verse, David portrays God as recording the details of his **wandering**. Here he speaks as if God had actually written in that **record** about the tears he has shed. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [After all, you are aware of them]

9.q: אָ֥֨ז יָ֘שׁ֤וּבוּ אוֹיְבַ֣⁠י אָ֭חוֹר בְּ⁠י֣וֹם אֶקְרָ֑א
9.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [On the day I call, then my enemies will turn back]

9.q: אָ֥֨ז יָ֘שׁ֤וּבוּ אוֹיְבַ֣⁠י אָ֭חוֹר בְּ⁠י֣וֹם אֶקְרָ֑א
9.note: See how you translated the similar expression “The day” in verse 3. Alternate translation: [When I call, then my enemies will turn back]

9.q: אָ֥֨ז יָ֘שׁ֤וּבוּ אוֹיְבַ֣⁠י אָ֭חוֹר בְּ⁠י֣וֹם אֶקְרָ֑א
9.note: David saying both **Then** and **on the day** (meaning “when”) for emphasis. However, in some languages this might seem to express extra information in a way that would not be natural. If so, you can use only one of these expressions. Alternate translation: [When I call, my enemies will turn back]

David means implicitly that he will **call** to God for help. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [I call to you for help]

The word that the ULT translates as **for** could introduce: (1) the reason why David knows that what he has just said is true. Alternate translation: [I know this because God is for me] or (2) the content of what David knows. Alternate translation: [This I know, that God is for me]

If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [Because God is for me, I know this]

10.q: בֵּֽ֭⁠אלֹהִים אֲהַלֵּ֣ל דָּבָ֑ר בַּ֝⁠יהוָ֗ה אֲהַלֵּ֥ל דָּבָֽר׃ בֵּֽ⁠אלֹהִ֣ים בָּ֭טַחְתִּי לֹ֣א אִירָ֑א מַה־יַּעֲשֶׂ֖ה אָדָ֣ם לִֽ⁠י
10.note: This is the second instance of the refrain in this psalm. (It occurs here in an expanded form.) We recommend that you show this to your readers by translating the phrases here the same way that you translated them in the first occurrence of this refrain in 56:4.

11.note: See how you translated the term “man” in 56:1. (Although David says **man** here where he said “flesh” in verse 4, the meaning is the same in both instances of this refrain.) Alternate translation: [What will people do to me?] or [Human beings can certainly do nothing to me!]

12.note: David is using **Your vows {are} on me** as a common expression of his culture to mean that he has made vows to God that he will publicly thank him for helping him and that he is bound by those vows to keep that promise. If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I am under vows to you] or [I have made vows to you]

David is using the possessive form to describe not vows that God has made but **vows** that he has made to **God**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [The vows I have made to you]

David is probably not referring to several different vows he has made to God. He probably means that he has made the same vow several times, that he will sacrifice a thank-offering to God when God delivers him. If your language uses a different plural form for a repeated action than it does for separate actions, it would be appropriate to use that form here. In some languages it may be natural to use a singular form. Alternate translation: [The vow I have made to you]

13.note: Here the word **For** does not introduce the reason why David is going to make a thank-offering to God. It introduces an explanation of why David is going to be able to do that. Use a connecting word or phrase in your language that will make this clear. Alternate translation: [I will be able to do this because]

It might seem that this expression contains extra information that would not be natural to express in your language. If so, you can shorten it. Alternate translation: [you deliver me from death] or [you rescue my life]

13.q: הֲ⁠לֹ֥א רַגְלַ֗⁠י מִ֫⁠דֶּ֥חִי לְ֭⁠הִֽתְהַלֵּךְ לִ⁠פְנֵ֣י אֱלֹהִ֑ים בְּ֝⁠א֗וֹר הַֽ⁠חַיִּֽים
13.note: David is using the question form to make a confident assertion. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [My feet are from stumbling, so I may walk about to the face of God in the light of the living!]

David is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [Are not my feet kept from stumbling] or, as an assertion, [You keep my feet from stumbling]

David is speaking as if God actually kept his **feet** from **stumbling**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Do you not keep me safe] or, as an assertion, [You keep me safe]
David is using the image of walking to represent living. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [that I may live]

Here, **to the face of** represents being in the presence of a person. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [in the presence of]

Here, **light** represents the earth, which people of this culture considered to be a light place, by contrast with Sheol, the realm of the dead, which was a dark place. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [in the world of the living] or [on this earth, where people are alive]

David is using the adjective **living** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [living people]
